nameStory: Carolina draba gets its name from the Carolina region where it was first scientifically described, though it actually grows across most of North America. The name 'whitlow-grass' comes from an old folk belief that this tiny plant could cure whitlows - painful infections around fingernails - even though it's not actually a grass at all but a member of the mustard family.
description: Carolina draba is a tiny annual wildflower that most people walk right past without noticing. This diminutive member of the mustard family grows only a few inches tall, forming small rosettes of narrow leaves close to the ground. Despite its small size, it produces delicate clusters of tiny white flowers that bloom early in the season, making it one of our earliest spring bloomers.

idTips.label: Flowers
idTips.description: Tiny white flowers with four petals arranged in a cross pattern, clustered at the top of thin stems - classic mustard family structure but requiring a close look to appreciate

idTips.label: Leaves
idTips.description: Small, narrow leaves arranged in a basal rosette, feeling slightly fuzzy to the touch and often with a few small teeth along the edges

idTips.label: Growth Habit
idTips.description: Extremely small annual plant, typically only 2-6 inches tall, easily overlooked among other vegetation

idTips.label: Fruit/Seeds
idTips.description: Develops small, flattened seed pods called silicles that split open when mature, releasing tiny seeds

habitat: Carolina draba is exceptionally rare in New England, found in open, disturbed soils and sandy areas. Look for it in sunny spots with thin soil, such as along roadsides, in fields, or other areas where competition from larger plants is reduced.

seasonality.spring: Blooms very early in spring with tiny white flowers, often one of the first mustards to flower when most other plants are just emerging.
seasonality.summer: Sets seed and may die back completely by mid-summer, as this annual completes its entire life cycle quickly.
seasonality.fall: Seeds germinate in fall, forming small rosettes that will overwinter and bloom the following spring.
seasonality.winter: Present as small, low rosettes of leaves that can survive freezing temperatures close to the ground.

funFact: Carolina draba is so rare in New England that it has only been documented once in the entire region - making any sighting a truly special botanical discovery that would excite researchers and naturalists alike!
confusionNotes: Its tiny white four-petaled flowers could be confused with other small mustards, but Carolina draba's extremely diminutive size and early blooming period help distinguish it. The key is looking for the classic mustard family cross-shaped flower pattern in a plant small enough to fit in your palm.
contextualKnowledge: Despite being called 'Carolina' draba, this plant actually avoids the southeastern states including the Carolinas themselves, creating a confusing gap in its range. The scientific name was recently changed from Draba reptans to Tomostima reptans, so you may see it listed under either name in field guides.
compareHints: Carolina draba is the only member of the genus Tomostima in our region. Compared to other small mustards like whitlow-grass (Draba species), Carolina draba tends to be even smaller and blooms earlier. Unlike the more common mustards such as winter cress or garlic mustard, Carolina draba stays tiny throughout its entire life cycle and never develops the taller flowering stems of its relatives.
